learningObjectives.title: The work of designers and companies

questions.q: In the ACCESS FM product analysis tool, what does the letter 'F' stand for?
questions.explain: In ACCESS FM the 'F' stands for Function, prompting the designer to consider what the product is meant to do.

questions.q: Which factor does the 'E' in ACCESS FM prompt a designer to evaluate?
questions.explain: The 'E' stands for Environment, encouraging consideration of a product's environmental impact and sustainability.

questions.q: What best describes primary research when analysing a product?
options: First-hand data the designer gathers themselves, such as user surveys or measurements
Data taken from existing books, websites and reports
Information supplied only by the manufacturer
questions.explain: Primary research is original, first-hand data collected directly by the designer, unlike secondary research which uses existing sources.

questions.q: Why is analysing existing products useful during the design process?
options: It helps identify strengths, weaknesses and opportunities to improve a design
It guarantees the new product will sell more units
It removes the need to write a specification
It automatically makes the product cheaper to manufacture
questions.explain: Analysing existing products reveals how well they meet user needs and highlights areas a new design could improve.

questions.q: A student carefully takes a kettle apart to see how its components fit together and how it is assembled. What is this activity called?
questions.explain: Taking a product apart to understand its construction and components is known as product disassembly.

questions.q: When evaluating a finished product, what does judging its 'fitness for purpose' mean?
options: How well the product performs the job it was designed to do
How attractive the product looks on a shelf
How much profit the product generates
How quickly the product can be manufactured
questions.explain: Fitness for purpose judges whether a product successfully carries out its intended function and meets its specification.

questions.q: A designer wants to assess whether a product's materials can be recycled at the end of its life. Which ACCESS FM heading covers this?
questions.explain: Recyclability and end-of-life impact are considered under the Environment heading of ACCESS FM.

questions.q: What does the term 'anthropometrics' refer to?
options: The measurement of human body sizes and dimensions
The study of how machines are manufactured
The testing of a material's strength
The measurement of a product's manufacturing cost
questions.explain: Anthropometrics is the collection and use of measurements of the human body to inform design.

questions.q: What does 'ergonomics' mean in design and technology?
options: Designing products so they are comfortable, safe and efficient for people to use
Choosing the cheapest possible materials for a product
Making a product look as attractive as possible
Testing how quickly a product can be mass-produced
questions.explain: Ergonomics concerns the relationship between people and the products they use, aiming for comfort, safety and efficiency.

questions.q: What does the 50th percentile represent in a set of anthropometric data?
options: The average measurement for the population
The smallest measurement in the population
The largest measurement in the population
A measurement that only 5% of people fall below
questions.explain: The 50th percentile is the mid-point of the data, representing the average person for that measurement.

questions.q: Why do designers often design products for the range between the 5th and 95th percentiles?
options: It accommodates about 90% of the population
It accommodates exactly half of all users
It only suits the tallest people
It removes the need to use average measurements
questions.explain: Designing between the 5th and 95th percentiles covers roughly 90% of users, a practical compromise for most products.

questions.q: A designer is deciding the height of a doorway so that people can walk through without ducking. Which percentile should the height be based on?
questions.explain: Clearance dimensions such as doorway height should suit the tallest users, so the 95th percentile is used.

questions.q: A designer is setting the height of a shelf so that as many users as possible can reach items on it. Which percentile should the reach be based on?
questions.explain: Reach dimensions should suit the smallest users, so the 5th percentile ensures shorter people can still reach.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of anthropometric data a designer might use?
options: The average hand grip width of adult users
The recyclability of a chosen plastic
The retail price of a competitor's product
The tensile strength of a steel bar
questions.explain: Anthropometric data are body measurements such as hand grip width, unlike material or cost data.

questions.q: Which product is James Dyson best known for developing?
options: The dual cyclone bagless vacuum cleaner
questions.explain: James Dyson developed the dual cyclone bagless vacuum cleaner, using cyclonic separation instead of a bag.

questions.q: Harry Beck is famous for designing which iconic piece of design?
questions.explain: Harry Beck designed the diagrammatic London Underground map in 1931, prioritising clarity over geographic accuracy.

questions.q: Which classic car was designed by Sir Alec Issigonis?
questions.explain: Sir Alec Issigonis designed the Mini, noted for its space-efficient transverse engine layout.

questions.q: The designer Dieter Rams is associated with which design philosophy?
options: 'Less, but better' - simple, honest and functional design
Designing products to break quickly so they are replaced
Prioritising low cost above all other factors
questions.explain: Dieter Rams, long associated with Braun, championed 'less, but better', favouring simple, functional and honest design.

questions.q: Philippe Starck designed the well-known 'Juicy Salif' citrus squeezer for which company?
questions.explain: Philippe Starck designed the iconic aluminium 'Juicy Salif' citrus squeezer for the Italian company Alessi.

questions.q: What is meant by 'market pull' when a company develops a new product?
options: A product is developed in response to consumer demand or a need in the market
A product is created purely to show off a new technology
A product is copied directly from a competitor
A product is designed only to reduce manufacturing cost
questions.explain: Market pull describes products driven by an identified consumer need or demand, in contrast to technology push.
